healthcare.summary: Health & medication guide for Poland. Emergency numbers (112/999/997/998), pharmacy tips, restricted medications, travel insurance advice, and vaccination recommendations.

recommended: tick-borne encephalitis (if hiking in forested eastern regions)
vaccinations.notes: No mandatory vaccinations. Ensure routine vaccinations are current. Eastern Poland has tick-borne encephalitis risk in forested areas during summer months.

pharmacy.hours: Most pharmacies open Mon-Fri 8am-6pm, Sat 8am-3pm. Some 24/7 pharmacies in major cities. Look for 'Apteka' signs — green cross.
pharmacy.tips: Pharmacists in tourist areas and major cities often speak English. Many common OTC medications are available. EU prescriptions are accepted. Poland has strong generic medication availability. Pharmacies in Poland can compound custom medications.

water.notes: Tap water is safe to drink throughout Poland. Polish tap water meets EU standards and is regularly tested.

healthcare.foodSafetyTips: Poland has good food safety standards. Traditional dishes like pierogi, bigos, żurek, and kielbasa are generally safe. Bigos (hunter's stew) is famously hardy and safe. Polish dairy (oscypek, bundz) at mountain stands is generally safe. Avoid unpasteurized milk from unregulated sources.

travelInsurance.requiredNote: Not legally required but strongly recommended for all travelers.
travelInsurance.tips: Poland is very affordable for healthcare — doctor visits, dental care, and medications cost a fraction of Western Europe. Travel insurance is still essential for emergencies and medical evacuation. Private clinics in major cities accept international insurance and have English-speaking staff.

healthcare.qualityNotes: Good quality healthcare, particularly in Warsaw, Kraków, and other major cities. Major cities have modern hospitals with increasing English-speaking staff. Rural areas may have fewer English-speaking doctors and older facilities. Private healthcare is affordable and widely available in cities.

medications.prescriptionRules: EU prescriptions are accepted. Prescriptions from outside the EU require a Polish doctor to re-issue them. Some medications available by prescription in other countries may be OTC in Poland.

restrictedMeds.name: Codeine-containing medications
restrictedMeds.note: Controlled. Requires prescription in Poland. Small personal-use quantities may be brought with proper documentation.

restrictedMeds.name: Tramadol
restrictedMeds.note: Controlled opioid. Requires prescription or doctor consultation. Carry your foreign prescription and doctor's letter.

restrictedMeds.name: Benzodiazepines
restrictedMeds.note: Controlled. EU regulations apply. Carry doctor's letter and original prescription and packaging.

restrictedMeds.name: Methylphenidate (Ritalin) and ADHD stimulants
restrictedMeds.note: Controlled. Requires documentation and possibly special permission. Contact Polish health authorities if traveling with ADHD medications.

restrictedMeds.name: Medical cannabis
restrictedMeds.note: Cannabis is illegal for recreational use. Medical cannabis is legal but strictly regulated. CBD products with no THC are legal and widely available.

medications.bringDocumentation: Carry a doctor's letter in Polish or English listing all medications with generic names. Keep medications in original packaging. EU citizens should carry EHIC. Non-EU travelers should carry original prescriptions and multilingual medical certificates.
medications.generalAdvice: Poland follows EU medication import regulations. Travelers from EU/EEA countries may bring personal-supply medications with a Schengen certificate for controlled substances. Non-EU travelers should carry prescriptions in original packaging with a doctor's letter. Polish pharmacies (apteka) are well-stocked and pharmacists are knowledgeable.

controlledSubstances.note: Medical cannabis is legal with a Polish prescription since 2017. Recreational use is illegal. CBD products with less than 0.2% THC are technically legal but enforcement is inconsistent — do not bring from abroad.
Controlled substances requiring a Schengen certificate (EU/EEA travelers) or doctor's letter (non-EU). Maximum 30 days' supply from non-EU countries.
Controlled under Polish narcotics law. Schengen certificate required for EU travelers. Non-EU visitors need a doctor's letter. Methylphenidate (Ritalin/Concerta) is available locally by prescription.
Controlled psychotropic substances. Requires Schengen certificate or doctor's documentation. Available locally with a Polish prescription.
Poland has banned numerous novel psychoactive substances following a crackdown on 'smart shops.' Penalties include up to 3 years imprisonment.
Illegal under Polish law. Possession of small amounts for personal use may result in dropped charges at prosecutor's discretion, but this is not guaranteed.

scams.name: The Horse Carriage Price Ambush
scams.description: The horse-drawn carriages around the Main Square look charming in all the photos, but tourists consistently report being quoted one price verbally and then handed a bill 3-5x higher at the end of the ride. The driver never clarified whether the price was per person or total, and somehow 'extras' ...

connectivity.simOptions: Play, Orange, or T-Mobile prepaid SIMs at airport shops or any 'salon' in the city. Cheap data — 20GB for ~30-40 PLN. Need passport.
connectivity.wifiAvailability: Free WiFi at most cafes, restaurants, hotels, and shopping malls. Quality is generally good. Many cities have free municipal WiFi.
connectivity.bestOption: Play prepaid SIM for best value and coverage. eSIM via Airalo or Holafly works well. EU roaming applies if you have an EU SIM.

cultural.tipping: 10% at restaurants is customary. Round up for taxis. Not expected at bars for simple drinks. Say 'reszta dla pana/pani' (keep the change).
cultural.dressCode: Smart casual in cities. Cover shoulders and knees in churches. Poland is quite fashionable — avoid looking too touristy.
cultural.greetings: Handshake with eye contact. Close friends kiss on both cheeks. Use Pan (Mr) / Pani (Mrs) until invited to use first names. Poles value politeness.
taboos: Confusing Poland with Russia or calling it Eastern Europe (it's Central Europe)
Making light of WWII or the Holocaust
Refusing food or drink when offered as a guest
Sitting at the corner of a table (superstition — won't marry for 7 years)
Giving even numbers of flowers (reserved for funerals)
cultural.haggling: Not practiced. Prices are fixed at shops, restaurants, and most markets.

safety.lgbtSafety: Poland has become increasingly challenging for LGBTQ+ travelers in recent years. Several municipalities declared themselves 'LGBT-free zones' (though these are being rolled back). Same-sex relationships have no legal recognition. Warsaw and Kraków are more tolerant, but discretion is advised, especially in smaller towns and eastern regions.
safety.soloFemaleSafety: Poland is generally safe for solo female travelers. Major cities like Warsaw, Kraków, and Gdańsk are well-traveled and have reliable public transport. Standard nightlife precautions apply — be cautious in entertainment districts and use registered taxis or ride-hailing apps.
safety.notes: Poland is a safe country for tourists with low rates of violent crime. Pickpocketing occurs in tourist hotspots like Kraków's Main Square and Warsaw's Old Town. Football hooliganism can occasionally affect city centers on match days. Overall, Poland offers excellent value and is very safe by European standards.

practical.visaFreeCountries: US citizens: 90 days visa-free (Schengen). UK, EU, Australia, Canada, Japan also visa-free.
practical.bestTimeToVisit: May-September (warm, long days). June-August peak season. December for Christmas markets. Avoid November (grey, cold).

immediate: Move away from rivers and low-lying areas during heavy rain
Do not drive through flooded roads
after: Report damage to WOPR (water rescue service) and local municipality

steps: File a police report immediately — get the report number, you will need it
Contact the US Embassy or nearest consulate: Contact the nearest US Embassy
Bring the police report + any ID you have (driver's license, copy of passport)
Apply for an Emergency Passport (usually issued within 1-2 business days)
Notify your travel insurance and airline of the situation
stolenPassport.notes: Keep a digital copy of your passport in cloud storage (Google Photos, iCloud) and email yourself a scan before travel.

steps: Go to the nearest police station (or call 997)
Bring ID or a copy of your passport if available
Request a written report — ask for an English copy or certified translation if needed
Keep the report number safe — required for insurance claims
For theft: list all stolen items with approximate values
policeReport.notes: In many countries, tourist police stations are available in major cities — they have English-speaking staff. Ask your hotel concierge for the nearest tourist police.

steps: If involved in an accident: do not move vehicles if anyone is injured
Call police (997) and ambulance (999) if there are injuries
Exchange contact, license, and insurance details with other parties
Document the scene with photos before moving vehicles
Contact your rental car company's emergency line
Contact your travel insurance's 24h assistance line
roadsideAssistance.notes: Traffic drives on the RIGHT. An International Driving Permit (IDP) is recommended for most foreign licenses. Rental vehicles are available at major airports and cities.
